title: The Equator and the Tropics
objective: After this level you can explain what the Equator, the tropics and the polar circles mark and why they sit where they do.
summary: The Equator splits the hemispheres. Earth's 23.5° tilt sets the tropics, the only zone with an overhead Sun, and the polar circles, where days can last 24 hours.

cards.headline: Twice a year in Hawaii, flagpoles lose their shadows at noon.
cards.body: The Sun stands straight overhead, and the shadow hides right under the pole. Anywhere else in the US? Never. A few imaginary lines on the globe explain why.

cards.headline: The Equator: Earth's belt
cards.body: Start in the middle. The Equator is 0° latitude, exactly halfway between the North and South Poles, and it splits the planet into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Twice a year, at the equinoxes, the Sun passes directly over it. Every latitude you met in Level 3 is counted from this line.

cards.headline: The tropics: where the Sun turns around
cards.body: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so the spot where the noon Sun stands directly overhead drifts north and south through the year. It reaches the Tropic of Cancer, about 23.5° N, around June 21. Then it turns back and reaches the Tropic of Capricorn, about 23.5° S, around December 21. Between those lines lie the tropics, the only places where the Sun is ever directly overhead. Hawaii is inside. The rest of the US is not.
cards.callout: Overhead Sun zone: 23.5° N to 23.5° S

cards.headline: The polar circles: days that last all day
cards.body: Now go about 23.5° from each pole: that same tilt again. You reach the Arctic Circle at about 66.5° N and the Antarctic Circle at about 66.5° S. On these lines the Sun stays up for a full day at least once a year, and stays down for a full day, too. Keep going toward a pole and it stretches to six months. Try explaining bedtime there in June.

cards.headline: Lines of light: learned
learned: The Equator is 0°, halfway between the poles
The tropics sit at about 23.5° N and S
Only in the tropics is the Sun ever overhead
Polar circles at about 66.5° get 24-hour days

questions.prompt: What does the Equator divide Earth into?

options.label: The tropics and the polar circles
options.rationale: Those are zones on each side of it.

options.label: Day and night halves
options.rationale: Day and night are set by the Sun, not a fixed line.

questions.explanation: The Equator, at 0° latitude, runs halfway between the poles and splits the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

questions.prompt: Why do the tropics lie about 23.5° north and south of the Equator?

options.label: That's how far ocean currents carry warm water
The 1884 conference chose those latitudes
options.rationale: That conference chose the prime meridian.

options.label: Mountains block the Sun beyond them
options.rationale: Mountains have nothing to do with it.

questions.explanation: Earth's tilt makes the overhead Sun drift up to about 23.5° north and south, so that's where the tropics sit.

questions.prompt: Using Level 3's latitudes, which town could have a day when the Sun never sets?

options.label: A town at 10° N
options.rationale: Far too close to the Equator.

options.label: A town at 23° S
options.rationale: That's near the Tropic of Capricorn, not a polar circle.

options.label: A town at 45° N
options.rationale: Close, but still south of the Arctic Circle.

questions.explanation: 70° N is north of the Arctic Circle (about 66.5° N), where the Sun stays up for at least one full day a year.
